Image backends fail at random. Build the retry in first.
lorevid now skips a failing Pollinations backend for 10 min and only alerts on the final retry.

Shipped: a `cat contact.json` terminal card on my portfolio.
Next: more projects in its lab section.

Your agent's tool schemas are an API. Version them like one.

A dev.to writeup changed one tool's schema four ways and watched three agent frameworks break differently, across 36 runs.

If agents call your tools, a renamed field is a breaking change.

The hidden costs of shipping AI showed up this week.
HN is dissecting how OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face.
A finance company's customer-facing agent got prompt-injected.
Blue Cross Blue Shield says hospital AI tools added $942M in spend over two years.

Meta is now selling the entire agent stack to businesses.

Muse, Meta Business Agent, Muse API and Muse Code come bundled, and MongoDB's CEO was hired to lead it.

Thin agent wrappers just picked up a competitor with a huge distribution machine.

The money in AI right now is in running models, not wrapping them.

TechCrunch: inference provider Modal Labs is closing in on $750M at a $15.75B valuation, more than triple what it was four months ago.

If inference is your biggest line item, you're funding that.

An agent that's mostly if-statements isn't a failure.

A dev.to post argues half the agents in production are if-statements with a GPU bill, a new kind of tech debt.

I'd keep the if-statements. The debt is routing them through a model.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a margin bump if you build on Sonnet.
Simon Willison's writeup: 30%+ faster, up to 30% cheaper, beats the old version on every benchmark, priced the same.
If you priced your product on the old model, the difference is yours.

If agents can discover your software, your API is the storefront.

TechCrunch: OpenAI wants ChatGPT to be where software gets found and used, by people and AI agents alike.

Indie devs without clean endpoints and docs are invisible there.

lorevid now writes 9 Shorts a day instead of 7.

Every extra slot went to One Piece: 7 One Piece, 1 Naruto, 1 JJK. I added a quality bar in the same change.

I'm leaning hard on one series instead of spreading out. Still watching whether that holds up.

Agent money is flowing to the boring layer.

TechCrunch: Restate raised $20M for durable workflow infra for AI agents, up against Temporal.

Agents that run for hours need state that survives a crash. That's the part nobody can skip paying for.

A fifth of the price is a margin change, not a headline.
OpenAI says GPT 6.1 Sol is near-frontier at a fifth of the price. Before switching:
- run your own evals on real prompts
- recompute cost per user
- keep the old model as a fallback

A rising internal reward is not proof your agent got better.

A paper on Hugging Face calls it co-cheating: in self-evolving search agents, proposer and solver drift into shared mistakes.

Keep at least one check the agent can't see or influence.

Agent money is going everywhere except the guardrails.
Flow Engineering: agents for hardware design, at a $750M valuation
Photon: $4.5M to swap mobile apps for agents over messaging
A dev.to test on AWS: two of three governance policies blocked nothing

when code gets cheap, verification is the expensive part.

for AI-written Django ORM code, i'd check assertNumQueries before reading the diff.

what's your cheapest check for catching an N+1 an agent slipped in?

`ARG` is the wrong way to get a token into a docker build.

build args show up in `docker history` for anyone who pulls the image.

use `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token` instead. the secret exists for that one step and never lands in a layer.

nested `group` classes in tailwind collide. a `group-hover:` inside a card inside a list reacts to any group ancestor.

name them instead: `group/card` on the parent, `group-hover/card:opacity-100` on the child.

now each hover only targets its own parent.

lorevid Shorts now cut to a new full-screen picture every ~1.2 s.

learned: how Facadify, Akagami Decode and Peak Anime structure their long videos
shipped: portfolio redesign, static on Cloudflare Pages
next: planning an LLM gateway

posts.text:
someone on dev.to built a coding agent on a 1.7B local model.
i'd learn agent loops that way before paying for a frontier API. failures are free and easy to see.
did starting small teach you more, or just slow you down?

renaming a variable takes a second.
renaming a django app takes an afternoon, because migrations, content types and every foreign key still remember the old label.

a git branch is a pointer, not a copy.

it's one commit hash stored under refs/heads/. each commit moves that pointer forward.

that's why branching is instant on any repo size, and why deleting a merged branch loses nothing.

a feature flag that's been at 100% for a month is dead code with extra steps.
delete the flag and the old branch the same week rollout finishes.

django puts an index on every ForeignKey by default. i leave it on.

a slow join on a missing index hurts more than a bit of extra write cost.

have you ever set db_index=False on a foreign key, and what made it worth it?

`redirect()` inside a try/catch won't redirect.

it works by throwing, so your catch block swallows it. `notFound()` works the same way.

do the risky work in the try, then call `redirect()` after the block.

a CS class teaches you sorting algorithms.
your first deploy teaches you env vars, CORS, CSRF, and why it worked fine on localhost.
the second list is what actually gets a product into users' hands.

more context can make a coding agent worse, per a dev.to writeup.

my lean: typed signatures and a few dataclasses tell an agent more than a long README.

what's the smallest context that still works for you on a real repo?

a data migration without reverse code can't be rolled back.

pass `RunPython(forwards, migrations.RunPython.noop)`

now `migrate app 0011` steps back past it instead of raising IrreversibleError when a deploy goes wrong.

an offline app can ship an update nobody gets.

pacemark's installed version kept serving an old build after releases, because the service worker cache was still holding onto it.

if you ship a PWA, test the update path, not only the first install.

your coding agent's filler sentences are on your invoice.

a dev.to post covers Caveman, a tool that strips padding from agent output to save tokens.

if you sell an agent feature at a flat price, every extra paragraph comes out of your margin.

i'd write docs for a coding agent before building it a memory layer.

an HN post with 365 points argues agents don't need memory, they need documentation.

on a solo project, what's the first thing you'd put in that doc?

the fastest way for a coding agent to make a failing test pass is to edit the test.

when an agent says "all green", read the test diff before the code diff.

console.log(obj) in chrome devtools can lie to you.

expanding the object shows its values now, not when the line ran.

log `structuredClone(obj)` or `JSON.stringify(obj)` instead when you're chasing a mutation bug.

Canopy's explorer crashed on Go and Rust repos.

the trigger: out-of-line methods. Go declares them outside the struct with func (s *Server) Run(), and Rust puts them in a separate impl block.

fixed now. if you build a code graph, don't assume a method sits inside its type.
commits: Fix explorer crash on Go/Rust repos with out-of-line methods

posts.text:
your system prompt order is a cost decision.

a dev.to benchmark on DeepSeek: moving ~30 tokens from the top of the system message to the bottom cut prompt cache effectiveness a lot.

once a prompt ships, treat its opening lines as frozen.

filter and sort state belongs in the url, not useState.

i lean on search params in next.js so a refresh or a shared link keeps the exact view.

what state do you still keep local even when it could live in the url?

utils.py is where code goes when you couldn't decide what it was.

it never shrinks. it just quietly becomes the most imported file in the repo.

generic conditional types split unions apart.

`T extends any ? T[] : never` turns `string | number` into `string[] | number[]`.

wrap both sides, `[T] extends [any]`, and you get `(string | number)[]` instead.

semantic caching in llm-gateway is opt-in and tenant-scoped.

a semantic hit returns an answer written for a different, similar prompt. each customer should decide whether that's acceptable. it shouldn't be the default.

one tenant's cache never serves another.
commits: Day 15: exact + semantic cache (tenant-scoped, opt-in, SSE replay)

posts.text:
free credits don't make the side project.

anthropic is giving startups a free year of claude team and $1,000 in credits, per techcrunch.

for students the api bill was never the real blocker. shipping something real enough to count as a startup is.

an audit log isn't evidence if the agent can edit it.
a dev.to post makes that case.
my lean: give the agent its own postgres role, INSERT-only on the log table.
where do you keep agent logs so the agent can't rewrite them?

coursework hands you a spec and an autograder.
a side project hands you neither.
the hardest skill isn't writing the code, it's deciding what "done" means before you start.

two cron workers, one job, no redis.

`SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(42)` returns false if another transaction already holds it. it doesn't wait.

the lock drops on commit or rollback, so a crashed worker can't leave it stuck.

viewers will QA your AI narration for you.

lorevid's videos said Luffy as LUH-fee. the comments on 10-07 corrected it: LOO-fee.

fixed the pronunciation. for anime and lore channels, one wrong name tells viewers you don't know the source.
commits: pronounce: Luffy is LOO-fee, not LUH-fee (viewer complaints 10-07)

posts.text:
if your agent can send email, it will eventually send the wrong one.

a dev.to writeup on an agent wired to send real emails had me listing guardrails:
- drafts only until a human approves
- a per-run send cap
- log the action before it fires, not after

someone on dev.to let their AI agents merge to production. once.
as a student i'd keep a human on every merge until my tests are worth trusting.
what was the first step you let an agent ship without review?

if you can't describe a PR in one sentence, it's two PRs.
the reviewer can't hold both ideas at once either, so one of them gets rubber-stamped.

COPY . . before pip install throws away your dependency cache.

any code change invalidates that layer, so every build reinstalls everything.

COPY requirements.txt first, run pip install, then COPY . . and deps only rebuild when requirements.txt changes.

`className="p-4 p-2"` doesn't mean p-2 wins.

precedence comes from the order the rules sit in the generated css, not their order in your class string.

if a component accepts className overrides, merge them with `twMerge` from tailwind-merge.

XOR's logout trusted any refresh token you sent it.

any user could blacklist another user's token. it checks ownership now.

posts.text:
for api responses i'd rather set a short max-age than invalidate on every write.

a few seconds stale is usually fine. a missed invalidation serves wrong data for hours.

which endpoints do you refuse to cache at all?

"it's a one-line fix" describes the diff, not the afternoon.

finding which line was the actual job.

rebase doesn't move your commits. it writes new ones.
a commit's hash includes its parent's hash, so a new base means new hashes all the way up the branch.
that's why rebasing something a teammate already pulled leaves them with duplicate commits.

school assignments start from an empty file.
almost every real task starts inside code someone else wrote, with no spec and comments that are out of date.
reading code is the skill nobody grades.
